props.title: The Wave

sections.content: The Wave (2008) stands as a chilling German drama that expertly demonstrates how easily fascism can take root in modern society. Based on a real 1967 California high school experiment, the film follows teacher Rainer Wenger as his classroom democracy simulation spirals dangerously out of control. Director Dennis Gansel's approach echoes the stark warnings found in Das Experiment (2001) and Lord of the Flies (1963), showing how group psychology can transform ordinary students into an authoritarian movement. The film's clinical precision makes it more disturbing than supernatural horror.

sections.content: The film connects thematically to other powerful explorations of conformity and resistance in schools, like Dead Poets Society (1989) and The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie (1969). But while those films show teachers inspiring individual thought, The Wave reveals how charismatic leadership can suppress it. The documentary The Corporation (2003) similarly examines how organizational structures can override individual moral judgment.

What makes The Wave particularly effective is its contemporary setting, suggesting fascism doesn't require brown shirts or jackboots to take hold. This connects it to modern political thrillers like V for Vendetta (2005) and Children of Men (2006), which also explore how democratic societies can slide into authoritarianism through small, incremental steps rather than dramatic coups. sections.content: The Wave sparked renewed interest in films examining social psychology experiments, leading to works like Compliance (2012) and The Stanford Prison Experiment (2015). These films share a documentary-like approach that emphasizes the banality of evil, showing how ordinary people can commit extraordinary acts under the right conditions. The Belko Experiment (2016) takes this concept to violent extremes, while Experimenter (2015) directly examines Stanley Milgram's groundbreaking obedience studies.
